name: Metoprolol Tartrate
whatItDoes: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate, blood pressure, and myocardial oxygen demand.
nurseActions: Check HR before administering — hold if HR <60 or per specific order
Check BP — hold if SBP <90 mmHg or per order
Monitor for bronchospasm in asthma/COPD patients
Do not abruptly discontinue — may cause rebound hypertension or angina
Monitor blood glucose in diabetic patients — may mask hypoglycemia signs
safetyNotes: May mask tachycardia as a sign of hypoglycemia
Contraindicated in decompensated HF, cardiogenic shock, severe bradycardia
Use caution in reactive airway disease

name: Lisinopril
whatItDoes: Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, preventing conversion of angiotensin I to II, resulting in vasodilation and reduced blood pressure. Also reduces cardiac remodeling in CHF.
nurseActions: Check BP before administering — hold if SBP <90 mmHg
Monitor K+ — ACE inhibitors cause potassium retention
Monitor renal function — creatinine and BUN
Assess for angioedema (throat swelling, lip swelling — rare but life-threatening)
Teach patient to rise slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension
safetyNotes: Contraindicated in pregnancy
Never combine with ARB — double blockade risk
Watch for dry cough (common side effect — may indicate need to switch to ARB)
Angioedema risk — particularly in Black patients

name: Furosemide
whatItDoes: Inhibits sodium-potassium-chloride transporter in the ascending loop of Henle, promoting diuresis. Reduces preload and fluid congestion in CHF and volume overload.
nurseActions: Monitor urine output — goal response: brisk diuresis within 30–60 min of IV dose
Monitor electrolytes — K+ and Mg2+ depletion common; replace per order
Monitor BP for hypotension
Weigh patient daily
Strict I&Os
Assess for dehydration signs
IV furosemide should be given slowly — max 4 mg/min to prevent ototoxicity
safetyNotes: High alert: ototoxicity risk with rapid IV infusion or large doses
Risk of profound diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances
Use with caution in sulfa allergy (cross-reactivity debate)
Hypokalemia can precipitate digoxin toxicity

name: Warfarin
whatItDoes: Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and proteins C and S. Used for thromboembolic prophylaxis/treatment. Long-acting — peak effect in 48–72 hours.
nurseActions: Check INR before administering — dose adjusted per INR result
Therapeutic INR for most indications: 2.0–3.0 (mechanical valves: 2.5–3.5)
Assess for bleeding: bruising, hematuria, melena, gum bleeding, headache
Hold and notify provider for INR >3.5–4.0 or signs of bleeding
Teach patient: consistent vitamin K diet, avoid sudden dietary changes, drug interactions
Do NOT crush or break tablets
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT medication — narrow therapeutic index
Multiple drug interactions (antibiotics, NSAIDs, azole antifungals increase effect)
Reversal: Vitamin K (slow), FFP or 4-Factor PCC (emergent)
Avoid IM injections in patients on warfarin

name: Heparin Drip (Unfractionated)
whatItDoes: Binds antithrombin III, inactivating thrombin and Factor Xa. Prevents clot extension and new clot formation. Requires aPTT monitoring for dose titration.
nurseActions: Obtain baseline aPTT, CBC, PT/INR before initiating
Draw aPTT 6 hours after initiation, after every rate change, then q6h when in therapeutic range
Therapeutic aPTT typically 60–100 seconds (confirm per facility protocol)
Assess for bleeding q4–8h: IV sites, urine, stool, neuro changes, back pain
Titrate per facility heparin protocol (weight-based preferred)
Never administer by IV push
Maintain platelet count monitoring — assess for HIT
Protamine sulfate available for reversal
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT medication
Never mix with other medications in same line
Two-nurse independent double-check of rate required per most facilities
HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia) risk — monitor platelets; if plts fall >50% from baseline on heparin, notify provider STAT
Bleeding risk — avoid IM, arterial punctures when possible
holdParameters: aPTT > 120 seconds — hold and notify provider

name: Insulin Regular (Drip)
whatItDoes: Exogenous insulin that facilitates cellular glucose uptake, reducing blood glucose. IV regular insulin has rapid onset (15–30 min) and short duration. Used for DKA, HHS, severe hyperglycemia, and post-cardiac surgery.
nurseActions: Monitor blood glucose per protocol — typically q1h
Target glucose range per order (usually 140–180 mg/dL for most ICU patients; 110–150 for cardiac surgery)
Titrate rate per protocol based on glucose trend (rising, stable, falling)
Replace potassium aggressively as insulin drives K+ into cells
Assess for hypoglycemia signs: diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, confusion
Have D50 at bedside
NEVER stop insulin drip abruptly without subcutaneous insulin coverage in place for DKA
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT medication
Insulin adsorption to IV tubing — flush tubing with insulin solution before starting (first 50 mL discarded per some protocols)
Hypoglycemia is the most serious immediate complication
In DKA: do NOT stop insulin until anion gap closed, even if glucose is normal — transition to D5 solution with insulin
holdParameters: Glucose < 70 mg/dL — hold, treat hypoglycemia, notify provider
Potassium < 3.3 mEq/L — hold insulin, replace K+ first

name: Norepinephrine (Levophed)
whatItDoes: Potent alpha-1 and beta-1 agonist causing significant vasoconstriction (increases SVR) with moderate positive inotropy. First-line vasopressor for septic shock. Maintains MAP and tissue perfusion.
nurseActions: Central line preferred — causes severe tissue necrosis if peripheral IV extravasates
If peripheral must be used: large-bore, AC or anticubital, check q1–2h for extravasation
Monitor MAP — goal typically ≥65 mmHg (confirm per order)
Monitor HR — watch for reflex bradycardia
Monitor urine output — marker of end-organ perfusion
Titrate per order (usually in increments of 0.02–0.05 mcg/kg/min)
Document rate changes with patient response
Wean slowly — check MAP before each decrease
Phentolamine at bedside for extravasation antidote
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT — critical care drug
Must be on continuous monitoring with alarm limits set
If extravasation occurs: stop infusion, inject phentolamine into affected area, notify provider
Taper slowly — abrupt discontinuation can cause hypotension
holdParameters: MAP > 90 mmHg consistently (assess for dose reduction)
Discuss with provider before holding — never abruptly discontinue

name: Dobutamine
whatItDoes: Primarily beta-1 agonist with mild beta-2 effects. Increases cardiac contractility (positive inotropy) and heart rate, improving cardiac output. Used for cardiogenic shock and acute decompensated heart failure with low cardiac output.
nurseActions: Monitor HR and BP continuously
Watch for tachycardia and arrhythmias — dose-dependent
Monitor cardiac output/index if PA catheter in place
Titrate per order based on hemodynamic response
Assess for worsening chest pain — increased O2 demand
Central line preferred
Wean slowly when discontinuing
safetyNotes: Can precipitate arrhythmias — especially at higher doses
May cause hypotension via beta-2 vasodilation
Not for use in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Increases myocardial O2 consumption — use caution in ischemic heart disease

name: Amiodarone
whatItDoes: Class III antiarrhythmic that blocks potassium, sodium, and calcium channels, and has alpha/beta adrenergic blocking properties. Highly effective for ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias.
nurseActions: IV loading dose followed by maintenance infusion per order
Must be given via dedicated IV line — incompatible with many drugs
Use in-line filter (1.2 micron) — amiodarone leaches DEHP from PVC tubing
Monitor EKG continuously for QT prolongation, bradycardia, AV block
Monitor BP — hypotension common with IV loading dose (slow the rate if BP drops)
Monitor LFTs, TFTs, PFTs with long-term use
Teach patient (long-term): sun protection, thyroid symptoms, pulmonary symptoms
safetyNotes: Extremely long half-life (40–55 days)
Multiple drug interactions including warfarin (increases INR), digoxin, statins
Pulmonary toxicity with long-term use
Thyroid toxicity (hypo or hyper) with long-term use
Phototoxicity

name: Vancomycin
whatItDoes: Glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. Used for MRSA, gram-positive infections, C. diff (oral only), and serious hospital-acquired infections.
nurseActions: Infuse over at least 60 min (1–2h preferred) — rapid infusion causes Red Man Syndrome
Monitor vancomycin trough or AUC per pharmacy protocol
Assess renal function — creatinine, BUN, urine output
Monitor for Red Man Syndrome: flushing, erythema, pruritus — slow infusion or premedicate
Check culture and sensitivity results to confirm appropriate coverage
Assess IV site for phlebitis — causes significant vein irritation
safetyNotes: Nephrotoxic — especially with aminoglycosides
Ototoxic at high levels
Red Man Syndrome is infusion-rate related — not a true allergy
Dose adjustment required for renal impairment
holdParameters: Discuss with provider/pharmacy if trough > 20 mcg/mL (traditional) or AUC out of range

name: Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs)
whatItDoes: Concentrated red blood cells that increase oxygen-carrying capacity. Each unit typically raises hemoglobin by ~1 g/dL and hematocrit by ~3%. Used for symptomatic anemia, active hemorrhage, or Hgb < 7–8 g/dL.
nurseActions: Two-nurse verification of patient ID, blood type, unit label at bedside — critical safety step
Obtain baseline vital signs before initiation
Start infusion slowly for first 15 minutes — stay with patient
Vitals at: baseline, 15 min, 30 min, q1h, and post-transfusion
Infuse over 2–4 hours per unit (never exceed 4 hours)
Transfuse through 18-gauge or larger IV, or blood filter tubing (170-260 micron filter)
Use only 0.9% NaCl to flush/piggyback — never dextrose
Stop immediately for any transfusion reaction and notify provider
Post-transfusion: check Hgb/Hct in 24h or per order
safetyNotes: Transfusion reactions: febrile non-hemolytic (most common), allergic, hemolytic (most dangerous — wrong blood type), TACO, TRALI
TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload): dyspnea, hypertension, crackles — slow transfusion, diuresis
TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury): acute respiratory distress 1–6h post-transfusion — supportive O2, notify blood bank
If reaction suspected: stop transfusion, maintain IV access with NS, notify provider and blood bank, save the blood bag
holdParameters: Any sign of transfusion reaction — STOP and assess

name: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)
whatItDoes: Contains all clotting factors. Used to reverse coagulopathy, warfarin overdose, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), massive transfusion, liver disease-related coagulopathy, or prior to invasive procedures in coagulopathic patients.
nurseActions: Two-nurse verification — ABO compatible (no Rh crossmatch required)
Thaw takes 20–30 min — plan ahead for urgent procedures
Infuse promptly after thawing — use within 24 hours if refrigerated at 1–6°C
Infuse as quickly as patient tolerates (usually 200 mL/hr unless fluid restricted)
Monitor for volume overload — TACO risk high (FFP is a significant volume load)
Vital signs per blood product protocol
Monitor coagulation studies post-infusion
safetyNotes: Volume overload risk — each unit is 200–300 mL
Allergic reactions possible
TRALI can occur with FFP
Do not mix with anything but NS via the same line
holdParameters: Signs of TACO or TRALI — slow or stop, notify provider

name: Platelets
whatItDoes: Platelet transfusion to prevent or treat bleeding from thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Each unit raises platelet count by ~10,000/μL.
nurseActions: Two-nurse verification
Infuse rapidly — over 15–30 minutes
ABO compatible preferred but not required
Do NOT refrigerate pooled platelets at bedside — must be kept at room temperature and agitated
Monitor for febrile non-hemolytic reactions (most common transfusion reaction with platelets)
Post-transfusion platelet count in 1 hour and 24 hours to assess increment
safetyNotes: Febrile reactions common — premedication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine may be ordered
HLA antibodies can cause poor platelet increment — inform blood bank if refractoriness suspected
Never irradiate standard platelets in most cases (irradiation for immunocompromised patients only)
holdParameters: Signs of systemic reaction — stop and assess

name: Cryoprecipitate
whatItDoes: Concentrated preparation from FFP containing fibrinogen, Factor VIII, Factor XIII, von Willebrand factor, and fibronectin. Used primarily for fibrinogen replacement in DIC, massive hemorrhage, or Factor VIII deficiency (when specific concentrate unavailable).
nurseActions: Two-nurse verification
Infuse within 4 hours of thawing
Infuse rapidly (over 15–30 minutes)
Monitor fibrinogen levels
ABO compatibility not required
safetyNotes: Small volume (10–20 mL per unit) — usually given as a pool of 10 units
Febrile and allergic reactions possible

name: Diltiazem Drip
whatItDoes: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows AV nodal conduction, reducing ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation and flutter. Also has vasodilatory effects.
nurseActions: Monitor HR and BP continuously
Goal typically HR 60–100 bpm or per specific order
Titrate per order (usually in 5 mg/hr increments)
Monitor for hypotension and bradycardia
Assess for signs of heart block
Wean slowly when discontinuing
Central line preferred for continuous infusion
safetyNotes: Contraindicated in WPW syndrome, decompensated HF, sick sinus syndrome without pacemaker
Can worsen CHF — assess lung sounds and edema
Drug interaction with simvastatin/lovastatin

name: Potassium Chloride IV
whatItDoes: Replaces potassium deficit and maintains normal intracellular potassium levels critical for cardiac, neuromuscular, and metabolic function.
nurseActions: NEVER give IV push — always infuse via pump
Peripheral IV: max 10 mEq/hr (causes severe vein irritation)
Central line: can infuse at higher rates per order
Administer via large-bore peripheral IV at a distal site — burning is common
Monitor IV site closely for phlebitis
Monitor EKG for peaked T waves (hyperkalemia) if giving large doses
Recheck K+ level 1–4h after infusion
Oral replacement preferred when patient tolerating PO
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT medication — IV potassium has caused fatal cardiac arrests when given undiluted or too rapidly
Never use concentrated KCl vials on nursing units (pharmacy dilutes)
Causes severe pain and phlebitis peripherally — consider central line for high doses or multiple replacements
holdParameters: K+ > 5.0 mEq/L — do not give, notify provider
Urine output < 30 mL/hr — potassium cannot be excreted; discuss with provider

name: Magnesium Sulfate IV
whatItDoes: Replaces magnesium deficit, stabilizes cardiac membranes, prevents seizures in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, and treats certain arrhythmias (torsades de pointes).
nurseActions: Administer via pump — not IV push for replacement
For hypomagnesemia replacement: typically 1–2 g in 50–100 mL NS over 1–2 hours
For pre-eclampsia: loading dose then maintenance per obstetric protocol
Monitor DTRs (deep tendon reflexes) — hypermagnesemia causes loss of reflexes before respiratory depression
Monitor respiratory rate, LOC, urine output
Have calcium gluconate (1 g IV) at bedside as antidote
Monitor EKG for PR prolongation, widened QRS
safetyNotes: Toxicity signs in order: loss of DTRs, somnolence, respiratory paralysis, cardiac arrest
Antidote: calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 3 minutes
Excreted by kidneys — use extreme caution in renal failure
Rapid infusion causes flushing, warmth, nausea

name: Morphine Sulfate
whatItDoes: Opioid agonist binding mu, kappa, and delta receptors, producing analgesia, sedation, and euphoria. Also reduces preload (useful in acute pulmonary edema) and has antitussive effects.
nurseActions: Assess pain using 0–10 scale before and 30 min after IV/IM, 1h after PO
Monitor respiratory rate — critical: hold if RR < 10–12
Monitor LOC, SpO2
Have naloxone (Narcan) available
Assess for bowel function — opioids cause constipation; initiate bowel regimen prophylactically
Assess urinary retention, especially post-op or in elderly
Start with lowest effective dose, especially in opioid-naive patients
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) requires specific monitoring
safetyNotes: HIGH ALERT — respiratory depression risk
Equianalgesic dosing when switching opioids (morphine 10 mg IV ≈ oxycodone 20 mg PO)
Renal failure: active metabolites accumulate — reduce dose/frequency
Elderly, opioid-naive: start low, go slow

name: Naloxone (Narcan)
whatItDoes: Competitive opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression, sedation, and analgesia. Acts within 2–5 minutes IV.
nurseActions: For opioid overdose: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/IN — repeat q2–3 min if no response (max 10 mg)
Titrate to adequate ventilation — not full reversal of analgesia (causes acute withdrawal/pain)
Monitor for re-narcotization — naloxone half-life is shorter than most opioids (30–90 min); may need repeat doses or infusion
Place patient in recovery position if unconscious
Continuous monitoring after administration
Prepare for withdrawal symptoms: agitation, tachycardia, vomiting
safetyNotes: Re-narcotization can occur when naloxone wears off — patient must be monitored for 2+ hours
May precipitate acute opioid withdrawal in dependent patients (agitation, pain, vomiting, diaphoresis)
Does not reverse benzodiazepine overdose

name: Aspirin
whatItDoes: Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing thromboxane A2 production and platelet aggregation. Low-dose used for antiplatelet therapy (ACS, stroke prevention); higher doses for anti-inflammatory.
nurseActions: Give with food or milk to reduce GI upset
Do not crush enteric-coated tablets
For ACS: 325 mg chewed immediately
Assess for GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis, hematochezia)
Hold if INR supratherapeutic in combination anticoagulation scenarios (per order)
safetyNotes: GI bleeding risk — especially with NSAIDs, steroids, anticoagulants
Contraindicated in children/teens with viral illness (Reye's syndrome)
Contraindicated in significant hepatic disease, active bleeding ulcers
Reye's syndrome risk in pediatric patients with viral illness

name: Clopidogrel (Plavix)
whatItDoes: Prodrug converted by CYP2C19 to active form that irreversibly inhibits P2Y12 ADP receptors on platelets, reducing platelet aggregation. Used for ACS, post-stent, stroke/TIA prevention.
nurseActions: Monitor for bleeding — assess IV sites, urine, stool
Hold per order for procedures (usually 5–7 days before elective surgery)
Give with or without food
Check for genetic polymorphisms in poor metabolizers (CYP2C19) — may need alternative
Do not combine with omeprazole (reduces efficacy) — use pantoprazole instead
safetyNotes: TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) rare but serious
Irreversible platelet inhibition — platelets must turn over (7–10 days) for full reversal
Drug interaction with proton pump inhibitors (esp. omeprazole)

name: Digoxin
whatItDoes: Inhibits Na-K-ATPase pump, increasing intracellular calcium and myocardial contractility (positive inotrope). Also slows SA and AV nodal conduction (negative chronotrope). Used for AFib rate control and systolic heart failure.
nurseActions: Check apical HR for full 60 seconds before giving — hold if HR < 60 bpm
Check dig level (therapeutic: 0.5–2 ng/mL; toxicity common above 2)
Assess for signs of toxicity: nausea/vomiting, anorexia, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos, blurred), bradycardia, arrhythmias
Check K+ level — hypokalemia potentiates toxicity
Give at consistent times
IV digoxin must be diluted (not undiluted)
safetyNotes: Very narrow therapeutic index — toxicity can occur within therapeutic range
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia all increase toxicity risk
Renal clearance — dose reduction in renal impairment
Many drug interactions (amiodarone, quinidine raise digoxin level)
Antidote: Digibind/DigiFab for severe toxicity
holdParameters: Signs of toxicity: nausea/vomiting, visual changes, new arrhythmia
K+ < 3.5 mEq/L (hold until repleted per order)

name: Pantoprazole (Protonix)
whatItDoes: Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase in gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion. Used for peptic ulcer disease, GERD, stress ulcer prophylaxis, and GI bleeding.
nurseActions: IV: infuse over 15 minutes (not IV push)
Give PO form 30–60 min before meals for best efficacy
Monitor Mg2+ with long-term use — PPIs cause hypomagnesemia
Assess for C. diff with prolonged use
Check for drug interactions — PPIs reduce absorption of certain drugs (clopidogrel interaction)
safetyNotes: Long-term use associated with: hypomagnesemia, bone fracture risk, C. diff, B12 deficiency
Recommended to use lowest effective dose for shortest time needed

name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
whatItDoes: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist that blocks serotonin both centrally and peripherally to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting.
nurseActions: IV dose given over 2–5 minutes (or per order — some facilities allow slow push)
Monitor EKG for QT prolongation at higher doses
Assess for constipation with repeated use
Effective for chemotherapy-induced, post-op, and general nausea
safetyNotes: Serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs
QT prolongation at doses > 32 mg/day
Limited use in patients with congenital long QT syndrome

name: Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
whatItDoes: Low-molecular-weight heparin that inhibits Factor Xa and, to lesser extent, thrombin. Used for DVT/PE treatment and prophylaxis, ACS, and bridging therapy.
nurseActions: Subcutaneous injection — pinch abdominal skin, 90-degree angle, do not aspirate, do not massage
Rotate injection sites — avoid within 2 inches of umbilicus
Do not expel air bubble from prefilled syringe (maintains precise dose)
Monitor anti-Xa levels for therapeutic dosing (not for prophylaxis)
Renal dosing adjustment for CrCl < 30 mL/min
Monitor for HIT (less common than unfractionated heparin but possible)
Hold for planned surgery/procedures per physician order
safetyNotes: NOT interchangeable unit-for-unit with other LMWHs
Protamine partially reverses (60–70% reversal)
Bioaccumulation in renal failure — dose reduce significantly or switch to UFH with monitoring

name: Nitroglycerin Drip
whatItDoes: Dilates venous capacitance vessels primarily (reduces preload) and, at higher doses, dilates arterial vessels (reduces afterload). Dilates coronary arteries. Used for unstable angina, acute MI, hypertensive urgency, and acute pulmonary edema.
nurseActions: Must use glass IV bottle and non-PVC tubing — nitroglycerin absorbs into PVC
Monitor BP every 5 minutes during titration, then q15–30 min when stable
Goal typically SBP within ordered range or symptom relief
Titrate per order (usually increments of 5–20 mcg/min q3–5 min)
Assess for headache (very common) — treat with acetaminophen
Monitor for tolerance with prolonged infusion (allow nitrate-free interval)
Use IV pump only
safetyNotes: Severe hypotension if given with PDE5 inhibitors (Viagra, Cialis) — contraindicated
Tolerance develops after 24h of continuous infusion
Can worsen hypotension in volume-depleted patients

name: Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl)
whatItDoes: Isotonic crystalloid solution used for fluid resuscitation, medication dilution, and maintenance hydration. Expands intravascular volume without changing intracellular volume.
nurseActions: Document rate and volume infused
Monitor for fluid overload: crackles, JVD, edema, worsening BP
Monitor electrolytes with large-volume infusion — hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis risk
Compatible with most IV medications for dilution
safetyNotes: Large volumes can cause dilutional hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Use with caution in CHF, renal failure, hepatic failure

name: Lactated Ringer's (LR)
whatItDoes: Isotonic balanced crystalloid solution containing electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Cl) and lactate. More physiologically similar to plasma than NS. Used for fluid resuscitation, especially in sepsis and trauma.
nurseActions: Monitor for fluid overload
Check compatibility before mixing with medications — LR incompatible with some drugs (amphotericin B, certain antibiotics)
Preferred over NS for large-volume resuscitation to reduce hyperchloremic acidosis risk
safetyNotes: Contains calcium — incompatible with blood products and some medications
Avoid in severe liver disease (cannot metabolize lactate)
Avoid in hyperkalemia (contains K+)

name: Dextrose 50% (D50)
whatItDoes: Concentrated glucose solution given IV to rapidly raise blood glucose in severe symptomatic hypoglycemia. Each 25 mL (12.5 g dextrose) typically raises glucose 25–50 mg/dL.
nurseActions: For unconscious or unable-to-swallow patients only — give glucose gel or OJ if alert and can swallow
Standard dose: 25–50 mL IV push over 1–3 minutes
Recheck blood glucose 15 min after administration
Treat underlying cause of hypoglycemia
Insulin patients: consider reducing insulin dose or adding longer-acting glucose source post-treatment
safetyNotes: MUST NOT be given IM/SQ — severe tissue necrosis
Vesicant — extravasation causes tissue damage; ensure IV is patent
Avoid in patients with hyperglycemia unless severe neurological symptoms from hypoglycemia override

name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
whatItDoes: Reduces fever by affecting hypothalamic heat-regulating center. Provides analgesia via central mechanism (exact mechanism not fully established). Does not inhibit prostaglandin synthesis peripherally — safe for GI tract.
nurseActions: Max dose: 4g/24h in healthy adults; 2g/24h in hepatic impairment or chronic alcohol users
Account for ALL acetaminophen from all sources — combination products (Percocet, NyQuil, etc.) contain acetaminophen
Give regularly (scheduled) for better effect than PRN in many situations
IV form: infuse over 15 min
safetyNotes: Hepatotoxicity at doses exceeding recommended maximums, especially with alcohol use
Hidden acetaminophen in many combination products — verify total daily dose
Do NOT use in acute liver failure
holdParameters: Hepatic impairment — check with provider for dose limit
